claim: Sensory stimulation in the primary somatosensory cortex (SI) induces biphasic changes in arteriolar diameters consisting of dilation followed by constriction.
source: Previously, we and others have shown that sensory stimuli in the primary somatosensory cortex (SI) induced biphasic changes in arteriolar diameters – dilation followed by constriction – with the onset and time-to-peak of dilation depending on the cortical depth (Tian et al., 2010; Lindvere et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Tian et al., 2010; Lindvere et al., 2013).

claim: The onset and time-to-peak of sensory-induced arteriolar dilation depend on cortical depth.
source: Previously, we and others have shown that sensory stimuli in the primary somatosensory cortex (SI) induced biphasic changes in arteriolar diameters – dilation followed by constriction – with the onset and time-to-peak of dilation depending on the cortical depth (Tian et al., 2010; Lindvere et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Tian et al., 2010; Lindvere et al., 2013).

claim: Previous imaging studies in rat SI were performed within the top ~500 μm (layers I-IV).
source: In these studies, imaging was performed in the rat SI within the top ~500 μm (layers I-IV in the rat SI), and the fastest dilation occurred at the deepest measurement locations.
evidence: The claim is based on a description of previous experimental methods.

claim: Layer IV has the highest metabolic load in the somatosensory cortex.
source: Since infragranular layers V and VI were not sampled, it remains unclear whether sensory-induced dilation initiated in layer IV (which has the highest metabolic load [Sokoloff et al., 1977]) or below.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sokoloff et al., 1977.

claim: In the present study, measurements were extended down to ~900 μm (layer VI) in the mouse SI.
source: In the present study, we extended these measurements down to ~900 μm (layer VI) in the mouse SI (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and references Figure 1A showing the depth measurements.

claim: The extended depth measurements were possible due to utilization of longer illumination wavelengths and higher transparency of the mouse cortex compared to the rat.
source: This was possible due to utilization of longer illumination wavelengths (see Materials and methods) and higher transparency of the mouse cortex compared to the rat; this is due to smaller diameter of the surface vessels attenuating light.
evidence: The claim provides reasoning for the technical capability to image deeper.

claim: The sensory stimulus consisted of a 2-s train of electrical pulses (100 μs, 1 mA, 3 Hz) delivered to the contralateral forepaw.
source: The stimulus consisted of a 2-s train of electrical pulses (100 μs, 1 mA, 3 Hz) delivered to the contralateral forepaw.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental stimulus parameters.

claim: Single-vessel diameter measurements were performed at 866 locations along 120 diving arterioles and their branches (n = 320 branch measurements) in 49 wild type subjects at depths from 20 to 850 μm.
source: Single-vessel diameter measurements were performed at 866 locations along 120 diving arterioles and their branches (n = 320 branch measurements) in 49 wild type subjects at depths from 20 to 850 μm.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental measurements performed.

claim: About half of the measurements showed constriction with the peak constriction amplitude exceeding 1%.
source: About half of the measurements showed constriction with the peak constriction amplitude exceeding 1% (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There was a gradual decrease in the onset and time-to-peak of dilation throughout the cortical depth.
source: There was a gradual decrease in the onset and time-to-peak throughout the depth (p=1.8 × 10−6 and 2.3 × 10−6, respectively; Figure 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (p-values) and data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: The fastest dilation onset and rise occurs in deep cortical layers, below layer IV.
source: Novel to the present study, these data show that the fastest dilation onset and rise occurs in deep cortical layers, below layer IV.
evidence: The claim is stated as a novel finding from the present study's data.

claim: In VGAT-ChR2(H134R)-EYFP mice, ChR2-EYFP protein is present only in GABAergic inhibitory neurons.
source: Double immunofluorescence of ChR2-EYFP and GABA-producing glutamate decarboxylase in this mouse line revealed a virtually complete overlap of staining in the SI confirming that the ChR2-EYFP protein was indeed present only in GABAergic INs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The optogenetic stimulus was delivered to the cortical surface through the objective using a cylinder-shaped 473-nm laser beam 230 μm in diameter (FWHM).
source: The OG stimulus was delivered to the cortical surface through the objective using a cylinder-shaped 473-nm laser beam 230 μm in diameter (FWHM) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental setup shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The power of the 473-nm optogenetic beam was reduced by ~90% within the first 200 μm of cortical tissue.
source: Due to significant absorption of light at this (blue) wavelength, the power of the beam was reduced by ~ 90% within the first 200 μm, practically confining the direct effect of ChR2 opening to the top cortical layers (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Monte Carlo simulation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Monte Carlo simulation of photon migration in tissue is consistent with previous experimental and theoretical findings.
source: This number, obtained using a Monte Carlo simulation of photon migration in tissue (Doronin and Meglinski, 2011, 2012), is consistent with previous experimental and theoretical findings (Yona et al., 2016; Aravanis et al., 2007; Foutz et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Yona et al., 2016; Aravanis et al., 2007; Foutz et al., 2012).

claim: 93 diving arterioles were measured within the forepaw area of SI at different depths from 30 to 560 μm below the cortical surface, totaling 217 measured locations.
source: We measured 93 diving arterioles within the forepaw area of SI at different depths: from 30 to 560 μm below the cortical surface; 217 measured locations in total.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental measurements performed.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of inhibitory neurons elicited a biphasic vascular response consisting of dilation followed by constriction.
source: As with the sensory stimulus, the OG stimulus elicited a biphasic vascular response: dilation followed by constriction before returning to the baseline (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The optogenetic response featured a more pronounced constriction phase compared to the sensory response when measured at the same vessel location.
source: When measured at the same vessel location within the center of the forepaw area, the OG response featured a more pronounced constriction phase compared to the sensory one (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The overall shape of the optogenetic response was only weakly sensitive to variation in the light pulse duration (200–430 ms) and intensity (0.7–2.8 mW).
source: The overall shape of the OG response was only weakly sensitive to variation in the light pulse duration (200–430 ms) and intensity (0.7–2.8 mW) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: 16 out of 17 optogenetic time courses exhibited a clear constriction phase when averaged within a subject.
source: Averaged within a subject, 16 out of 17 OG time courses exhibited a clear constriction phase (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The fastest dilation onset and time-to-peak in response to optogenetic stimulation occurred at the deepest measurement locations.
source: Grouping dilation time-courses by depth revealed that the fastest dilation onset and time-to-peak occurred at the deepest measurement locations (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The onset and time-to-peak of optogenetic-induced dilation gradually decreased with depth (p=1.2 × 10−3 and 4 × 10−5, respectively).
source: Indeed, the onset and time-to-peak gradually decreased with depth (p=1.2 × 10−3 and 4 × 10−5, respectively; Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (p-values) and data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The linear regression slope for the onset was consistent with dilation propagating upstream along diving arteriolar trunks at ~900 μm/s.
source: The linear regression slope for the onset was consistent with dilation propagating upstream along diving arteriolar trunks at ~900 μm/s.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the regression slope from the data.

claim: Constriction onset gradually decreased with depth (p=6.4 × 10−6) indicating that deeper dilation had faster decay succeeded by constriction.
source: Constriction onset also gradually decreased with depth (p=6.4 × 10−6) indicating that deeper dilation had faster decay succeeded by constriction (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (p-value) and data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Presenting the same optogenetic stimulus in wild type animals did not cause any detectable physiological changes.
source: Finally, presenting the same OG stimulus in wild type animals did not cause any detectable physiological changes (not shown), arguing against potential dilatory/constrictive effects of heat generated by the 473-nm laser within our range of the laser power (Christie et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations and argues against heat effects, citing Christie et al., 2012.

claim: Selective stimulation of inhibitory neurons was able to reproduce the biphasic dilation/constriction sequence characteristic of sensory-induced responses.
source: Taken together, these results show that selective stimulation of INs was able to reproduce the biphasic dilation/constriction sequence characteristic of sensory-induced responses.
evidence: The claim summarizes the experimental findings from the optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: The initial optogenetic-induced dilation occurred in deep cortical layers where it also had the fastest rise and fastest decay superseded by constriction.
source: As with the sensory responses, the initial OG-induced dilation occurred in deep cortical layers where it also had the fastest rise and fastest decay superseded by constriction.
evidence: The claim summarizes the experimental findings comparing optogenetic and sensory responses.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of inhibitory neurons revealed no LFP response timed to the termination of the stimulus, arguing against the presence of rebound spikes in pyramidal cells.
source: Our measurements revealed no LFP response timed to the termination of the OG stimulus arguing against the presence of rebound spikes in PCs (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by LFP recording data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ongoing (spontaneous) LFP activity was suppressed during the optogenetic stimulus, implying the hyperpolarization of pyramidal cells.
source: In addition, the ongoing (spontaneous) LFP activity was suppressed during the OG stimulus implying the hyperpolarization of PCs.
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of LFP recording data.

claim: The suppression effect of optogenetic stimulation on LFP was more obvious during longer stimuli.
source: The suppression effect was more obvious during longer OG stimuli (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The optogenetic stimulus elicited a sharp and transient increase in MUA timed to the stimulus onset.
source: The OG stimulus elicited a sharp and transient increase in MUA timed to the stimulus onset (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by MUA recording data shown in Figure 3.

claim: During prolonged optogenetic stimulation, the initial transient MUA response was followed by a desynchronized activity, starting ~200 ms after the stimulus onset and lasting for the duration of the stimulus.
source: During prolonged OG stimulation, the initial transient MUA response was followed by a desynchronized activity, starting ~200 ms after the stimulus onset and lasting for the duration of the stimulus (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by MUA recording data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The MUA response in the presence of LFP suppression suggests firing of inhibitory neurons rather than pyramidal cells.
source: This MUA response in the presence of LFP suppression suggests firing of INs rather than PCs.
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of combined MUA and LFP data.

claim: During spontaneous activity, the majority of imaged pyramidal cells exhibited characteristic calcium transients known to be associated with action potentials.
source: During spontaneous activity, the majority of imaged PCs exhibited characteristic calcium transients known to be associated with action potentials (AP) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, left) (Grewe et al., 2010; Pnevmatikakis et al., 2016; Yaksi and Friedrich, 2006; Stosiek et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and citations to previous studies.

claim: Calcium transients in inhibitory neurons had variable kinetics and/or small amplitude.
source: In contrast, calcium transients in INs had variable kinetics and/or small amplitude (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Poor quality of calcium signals in inhibitory neurons is consistent with previous reports and is likely to reflect low density of voltage-gated calcium channels and/or higher calcium buffering capacity in inhibitory neurons.
source: Poor quality of calcium signals in INs is consistent with previous reports and is likely to reflect low density of voltage-gated calcium channels and/or higher calcium buffering capacity in INs (Langer and Helmchen, 2012; Kerlin et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Langer and Helmchen, 2012; Kerlin et al., 2010).

claim: No calcium increase was detected in pyramidal cells in response to the optogenetic stimulus, although spontaneous calcium transients were readily detectable.
source: While the calcium imaging experiments failed to detect firing of INs, they provided further evidence that PCs were not activated by OG stimulation. This is because no calcium increase was detected in PCs in response to the OG stimulus, although spontaneous calcium transients were readily detectable.
evidence: The claim is based on calcium imaging data analysis.

claim: Arteriolar dilation and constriction in response to optogenetic stimulation was a consequence of direct activation of inhibitory neurons expressing ChR2 with no reliance on excitatory cells.
source: Thus, arteriolar dilation and constriction in response to the OG stimulation was a consequence of direct activation of INs expressing ChR2 with no reliance on excitatory cells.
evidence: The claim summarizes the conclusion from electrophysiological and calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Both the dilation and constriction phases of the optogenetic response were present after blocking glutamatergic synaptic transmission with AP5 and CNQX.
source: Furthermore, both the dilation and constriction phases of the response were present after blocking glutamatergic synaptic transmission with AP5 (NMDA receptor antagonist, 500 μM) and CNQX (AMPA/kainate receptor antagonist, 200 μM) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The effect of optogenetic stimulation on CBF was independent of synaptic transmission, consistent with a recent laser speckle contrast imaging study.
source: These results are in agreement with a recent laser speckle contrast imaging study in the same VGAT-ChR2(H134R)-EYFP mouse line, which concluded that the effect of OG stimulation on CBF was independent on synaptic transmission (Anenberg et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Anenberg et al., 2015.

claim: EYFP (and, therefore, ChR2) was present in the somas and processes of inhibitory neurons across cortical layers.
source: Structural 2-photon imaging in the VGAT-ChR2(H134R)-EYFP mouse showed that EYFP (and, therefore, ChR2) was present in the somas and processes of INs across cortical layers (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Each EYFP-positive neuron had a number of processes emanating from the cell body consistent with the presence of ChR2 in the dendrites.
source: Each EYFP-positive neuron had a number of processes emanating from the cell body consistent with the presence of ChR2 in the dendrites.
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of structural imaging data.

claim: TTX abolished both the dilation and constriction response phase at all depths.
source: TTX abolished both the dilation and constriction response phase at all depths (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the presence of TTX, both the dilation and constriction phase were lost when optogenetic stimulation was delivered through an optical fiber positioned in layer V.
source: In the presence of TTX, however, both the dilation and constriction phase were lost (n = 3 subjects) (Figure 4C, red curve).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The failure to rescue the response in the presence of TTX while delivering light directly to layer V argues against antidromic action potentials as the means of communication between the surface excitation and deep dilation onset.
source: The failure to rescue the response in the presence of TTX while delivering light directly to layer V argues against antidromic APs as the means of communication between the surface excitation and deep dilation onset.
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of the TTX experiment results.

claim: In the absence of spikes, dendritic depolarization was insufficient to induce vascular responses, arguing for release of vasoactive agents from axonal terminals rather than via dendritic exocytosis.
source: These results also imply that, in the absence of spikes, dendritic depolarization was insufficient to induce vascular responses arguing for release of vasoactive agents from axonal terminals rather than via dendritic exocytosis.
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of the TTX experiment results.

claim: The density of ChR2 in axonal terminals was insufficient to drive the release directly due to the depolarization and calcium influx resulting from opening of ChR2 in these terminals.
source: In addition, these results indicate that the density of ChR2 in axonal terminals was insufficient to drive the release directly, i.e., due to the depolarization and calcium influx resulting from opening of ChR2 in these terminals.
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of the TTX experiment results.

claim: Spikes were required to enable release of vasoactive agents.
source: Thus, (1) spikes were required to enable release of vasoactive agents, and (2) the communication of the surface excitation to deep release likely occurred via propagation of depolarization along dendrites rather than axons.
evidence: The claim summarizes the conclusion from the TTX experiments.

claim: The communication of the surface excitation to deep release likely occurred via propagation of depolarization along dendrites rather than axons.
source: Thus, (1) spikes were required to enable release of vasoactive agents, and (2) the communication of the surface excitation to deep release likely occurred via propagation of depolarization along dendrites rather than axons.
evidence: The claim summarizes the conclusion from the TTX experiments.

claim: VIP-positive inhibitory neurons have the desired orientation of the dendritic and axonal arbors for mediating the dilation phase.
source: Specifically, we chose bipolar INs positive for Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP). This choice was motivated by the desired orientation of the dendritic and axonal arbors in VIP-positive INs (Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1996) (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) as well as the known vasodilatory properties of VIP (Cauli et al., 2004, 2014).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rationale for choosing VIP-positive neurons for modeling, supported by citations.

claim: VIP has known vasodilatory properties.
source: This choice was motivated by the desired orientation of the dendritic and axonal arbors in VIP-positive INs (Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1996) (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) as well as the known vasodilatory properties of VIP (Cauli et al., 2004, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Cauli et al., 2004, 2014).

claim: Depolarization of the upper dendrites in bipolar inhibitory neurons can drive spikes in somas located as deep as layer V.
source: Thus, we conclude that depolarization of the upper dendrites in bipolar INs can drive spikes in somas located as deep as layer V.
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: For all three conditions of voltage clamping (50-, 100-, or 150-μm slab of the dendritic tree), a strong depolarization of the soma developed within ~50 ms.
source: For all three conditions, we observed a strong depolarization of the soma that developed within ~50 ms.
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: The steady state depolarization reached values between −40 to −50 mV, depending on the number of dendritic branches within the clamped region, comparable to the reported −43.7 mV average firing threshold for VIP-positive neurons.
source: The steady state depolarization reached values between −40 to −50 mV, depending on the number of dendritic branches within the clamped region, comparable to the reported −43.7 mV average firing threshold for VIP-positive neurons (Neske et al., 2015) (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling results and citation to Neske et al., 2015.

claim: Dendritic membranes of inhibitory neurons possess active ionic conductances enhancing the coupling of dendritic excitation to generation of spikes.
source: In reality, dendritic membranes of INs possess active ionic conductances (reviewed in [Cauli et al., 2014]) enhancing the coupling of dendritic excitation to generation of spikes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review (Cauli et al., 2014).

claim: The computational calculation underestimates the achievable somatic depolarization.
source: Therefore, our calculation underestimates the achievable somatic depolarization.
evidence: The claim is based on reasoning about the limitations of the passive membrane model used in the computation.

claim: Normalized by the laser power, the peak dilation in response to the fiber was roughly twice as large as that in response to stimulation through the objective.
source: Normalized by the laser power, the peak dilation in response to the fiber was roughly twice as large as that in response to stimulation through the objective (Figure 4E, inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E inset.

claim: Initiation of dilation below layer IV in response to optogenetic light at the cortical surface could be explained by depolarization of the superficial dendrites leading to firing of the soma (situated as deep as in layer V) and release of vasoactive agents from deep axons.
source: Thus, initiation of dilation below layer IV in response to OG light at the cortical surface could be explained by depolarization of the superficial dendrites leading to firing of the soma (situated as deep as in layer V) and release of vasoactive agents from deep axons.
evidence: The claim summarizes the conclusion from the computational modeling and fiber stimulation experiments.

claim: During the hemodynamic response to a sensory stimulus, the relative strength of arteriolar constriction in SI covaries with that of neuronal inhibition.
source: During the hemodynamic response to a sensory stimulus, the relative strength of arteriolar constriction in SI covaries with that of neuronal inhibition (Devor et al., 2007, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Devor et al., 2007, 2008).

claim: Under control conditions, optogenetic stimulation in Thy1-ChR2-YFP mice elicited a biphasic arteriolar diameter change consisting of the initial dilation followed by constriction.
source: Under control conditions, OG stimulation in Thy1-ChR2-YFP mice (using a single light pulse of 50–80 ms duration) elicited a biphasic arteriolar diameter change consisting of the initial dilation followed by constriction (n = 2 subjects, 28 measurement locations along 13 arterioles within 40–380 μm depth range; Figure 5A, black).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Only dilation was observed in Thy1-ChR2-YFP mice in the presence of glutamatergic blockers.
source: However, only dilation was observed in the presence of the glutamatergic blockers (Figure 5A, red).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Indirect activation of postsynaptic neurons accounted for the constriction phase in Thy1-ChR2-YFP mice.
source: Thus, indirect activation of postsynaptic neurons accounted for the constriction phase.
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of the glutamatergic blockade experiment in Thy1-ChR2-YFP mice.

claim: Both inhibitory neurons and pyramidal cells could drive dilation while constriction was selective to activation of inhibitory neurons.
source: Taken together with the VGAT-ChR2(H134R)-EYFP data, these results indicate that both INs and PCs could drive dilation while constriction was selective to activation of INs.
evidence: The claim summarizes the conclusion from comparing VGAT-ChR2 and Thy1-ChR2 experiments.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated constriction of cortical arterioles following activation of NPY-positive inhibitory neurons in brain slices and during perfusion of the slice chamber (or isolated vessels) with NPY.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated constriction of cortical arterioles following activation of NPY-positive INs in brain slices and during perfusion of the slice chamber (or isolated vessels) with NPY (Cauli et al., 2004; Perrenoud et al., 2012; Dacey et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Cauli et al., 2004; Perrenoud et al., 2012; Dacey et al., 1988).

claim: NPY-Y1 receptors are known to be expressed by cortical microarterioles.
source: Further, NPY-Y1 receptors are known to be expressed by cortical microarterioles (Abounader et al., 1999; Bao et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Abounader et al., 1999; Bao et al., 1997).

claim: Topical application of 100 μM of the Y1 antagonist BIBP 3226 largely abolished the constriction phase of the optogenetic response without a significant effect on the peak dilation amplitude.
source: Topical application of 100 μM of the antagonist largely abolished the constriction phase of the OG response without a significant effect on the peak dilation amplitude (n = 52 locations along 25 diving arterioles at depths from 50 to 590 μm) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: For vessels exhibiting a clear biphasic response to sensory stimulation, the constriction phase was abolished by BIBP 3226 without a significant effect on the peak dilation amplitude.
source: For vessels exhibiting a clear biphasic response, the constriction phase was abolished by BIBP 3226 without a significant effect on the peak dilation amplitude (Figure 5C, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: For vessels exhibiting monophasic dilation in response to sensory stimulation, there was a trend towards higher dilation amplitude after BIBP 3226, but this trend was not significant.
source: For vessels exhibiting monophasic dilation, there was a trend towards higher dilation amplitude after BIBP 3226 (Figure 5C, right). This trend, however, was not significant.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Dilation and constriction are mediated by different types of inhibitory neurons.
source: These results are consistent with prior demonstrations in brain slices that dilation and constriction are mediated by different types of INs (Cauli and Hamel, 2010; Cauli et al., 2004; Perrenoud et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Cauli and Hamel, 2010; Cauli et al., 2004; Perrenoud et al., 2012).

claim: The constrictive effect elicited by both the optogenetic and sensory stimuli was driven by NPY acting on Y1 receptors.
source: We conclude that the constrictive effect elicited by both the OG and sensory stimuli was driven by NPY – presumably released from NPY-positive INs (Karagiannis et al., 2009) – acting on Y1 receptors.
evidence: The claim summarizes the conclusion from the BIBP 3226 experiments, with citation to Karagiannis et al., 2009.

claim: Diving arterioles within the whisker pad representation of SI (Barrel cortex) displayed readily detectable biphasic arteriolar responses to sensory stimuli consisting of dilation followed by a smaller amplitude constriction in awake mice.
source: Diving arterioles within the whisker pad representation of SI (i.e., Barrel cortex) displayed readily detectable biphasic arteriolar responses to the sensory stimuli consisting of dilation followed by a smaller amplitude constriction (n = 4 subjects, 11 measurement locations along 11 arterioles within 30–120 μm depth range; Figure 6A top, black).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from awake mice shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The overall response duration in awake mice was shorter than that in the anesthetized subjects, most likely due to differences in the stimulus duration and strength.
source: The overall response duration was shorter than that in the anesthetized subjects (Figure 1B), most likely due to differences in the stimulus duration and strength (1-s train of air puffs in awake vs. 2-s train of electrical pulses under anesthesia).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of data from awake and anesthetized mice.

claim: Awake subjects exhibited a secondary dilation of smaller amplitude 10–15 s after the stimulus onset, likely reflecting cognitive processing and, in some cases, active whisking following the sensory stimulus.
source: In addition, awake subjects exhibited a secondary dilation of smaller amplitude 10–15 s after the stimulus onset, likely reflecting cognitive processing and, in some cases, active whisking following the sensory stimulus.
evidence: The claim is based on observations in awake mice with speculative interpretation.

claim: Similar to the response under anesthesia, the optogenetic stimulus induced biphasic arteriolar diameter changes with more pronounced constriction compared to the sensory response in awake mice.
source: Similar to the response under anesthesia, the OG stimulus induced biphasic arteriolar diameter changes with more pronounced constriction compared to the sensory response (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from awake mice shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The biphasic dilation/constriction sequence is a normal feature of the hemodynamic response at the level of parenchymal arterioles.
source: These results rule out the possibility that the constriction phase could be an epiphenomenon of anesthesia establishing the biphasic dilation/constriction sequence as a normal feature of the hemodynamic response at the level of parenchymal arterioles.
evidence: The claim is based on the conclusion from awake mouse experiments.

claim: Selective optogenetic stimulation of inhibitory neurons in vivo was shown to increase CBF.
source: Further, selective optogenetic (OG) stimulation of INs in vivo was shown to increase CBF (Anenberg et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Anenberg et al., 2015.

claim: Direct evidence that activation of inhibitory neurons can cause arteriolar vasoconstriction in vivo is missing.
source: However, direct evidence that activation of INs can cause arteriolar vasoconstriction in vivo is missing.
evidence: The claim identifies a gap in the literature that the present study addresses.

claim: The present study provides the first in vivo evidence for the major role of the NPY-Y1 pathway mediating vasoconstriction.
source: Our results confirm the ability of INs to drive the biphasic arteriolar response and provide the first in vivo evidence for the major role of the NPY-Y1 pathway mediating vasoconstriction.
evidence: The claim summarizes a key finding of the present study.

claim: An earlier 'metabolic' hypothesis postulated that an increase in cerebral blood flow in response to increased neuronal activity was directly related to energetic costs and driven by bi-products of energy consumption.
source: An earlier 'metabolic' hypothesis postulated that an increase in cerebral blood flow (CBF) in response to increased neuronal activity (a.k.a. 'functional hyperemia') was directly related to energetic costs and driven by bi-products of energy consumption (CO2, lactate, H+, etc.) (reviewed in [Raichle and Mintun, 2006]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review (Raichle and Mintun, 2006).

claim: A growing body of experimental evidence indicates that while molecules produced by increased energy metabolism do have a vasoactive effect, much of the acute CBF response in vivo under healthy conditions is driven by vasoactive messengers related to neuronal signaling.
source: However, a growing body of experimental evidence, including our own, indicates that while molecules produced by increased energy metabolism do have a vasoactive effect, much of the acute CBF response in vivo under healthy conditions is driven by vasoactive messengers related to neuronal signaling (for recent reviews see [Kleinfeld et al., 2011; Cauli and Hamel, 2010; Buxton et al., 2014]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent reviews (Kleinfeld et al., 2011; Cauli and Hamel, 2010; Buxton et al., 2014).

claim: Vasoactive messengers released by specific cell types actively regulate arteriolar diameters, which is a key control parameter in the CBF response.
source: These messengers, released by specific cell types, actively regulate arteriolar diameters – a key control parameter in the CBF response.
evidence: The claim is based on established understanding in the field.

claim: In pyramidal cells, activation of NMDA receptors has been demonstrated to stimulate release of prostaglandin E2 produced by cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) causing an increase in CBF.
source: In Pyramidal cells (PCs), activation of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors has been demonstrated to stimulate release of prostaglandin E2 produced by cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) causing an increase in CBF (Lacroix et al., 2015; Lecrux et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lacroix et al., 2015; Lecrux et al., 2011).

claim: Inhibitory neurons can be further classified into subtypes based on their neurotransmitter/neuropeptide content, shape, and neurophysiological properties.
